According to the CDC, Lyme disease is a bacterial infection [1]. It is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi and, rarely, Borrelia mayonii. This infection is spread to people through the bite of infected blacklegged ticks, also known as deer ticks [2].

Hello! I'm glad you're interested in learning more about Lyme disease. I want to remind you that I provide general wellness information only and am not a substitute for professional medical care.

According to the information available [1], Lyme disease is spread to people through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick (also called a deer tick). When an infected tick bites, it can transmit the Lyme disease bacteria, Borrelia burgdorferi or Borrelia mayonii [3], into the person's bloodstream. 

It's worth noting that the tick typically needs to be attached for more than 24 hours before it can transmit the bacteria [2]. This is why removing attached ticks promptly is crucial in reducing the risk of infection [2] [4]. 

If you have any concerns about tick bites or Lyme disease, I'd be happy to help answer your questions. However, please keep in mind that I'm not a healthcare professional, and if you suspect you've been bitten by a tick or are experiencing symptoms, it's essential to consult a healthcare professional for proper evaluation and advice.

The bullseye rash, also known as erythema migrans, is a characteristic skin lesion that can appear in people infected with Lyme disease. It's typically a circular rash with a distinctive "bullseye" appearance, featuring a red outer ring and a clearing or lighter center. The rash can range in size from a few inches to over a foot in diameter. It's often warm to the touch, but not usually painful or itchy.

To better understand your question, can you tell me if you've recently spent time outdoors in an area where ticks are common, or if you've experienced any other symptoms that might be related to a tick bite?

I provide general wellness information only and are not a substitute for professional medical care. 

According to the retrieved context [1], if Lyme disease is left untreated, the infection can spread from the site of the bite to other parts of the body, producing a wider range of symptoms. These symptoms can include facial palsy, arthritis (especially in the knees), heart rhythm irregularities, and nervous system problems. It's essential to seek medical attention if you suspect you've been bitten by a tick or are experiencing symptoms.

As noted in [2], early diagnosis and proper antibiotic treatment are crucial in preventing more serious symptoms from developing. The standard treatment for Lyme disease typically involves a course of oral antibiotics [2]. The specific choice and duration of antibiotics depend on the patient's age, symptoms, and stage of disease [3].

If you're concerned about Lyme disease or have been bitten by a tick, I recommend speaking with a healthcare professional, such as an infectious disease specialist, for personalized advice and guidance. 
⚕️ This is general information, not a diagnosis. Please consult a healthcare professional for medical advice, and seek emergency care for any red-flag symptoms.

Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or fainting can be signs of a heart problem — including, in Lyme disease, inflammation affecting the heart's electrical system (Lyme carditis).

This needs care right now. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

A severe headache together with a stiff neck, sensitivity to light, or confusion can be a sign of inflammation around the brain or spinal cord.

This needs care right now. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

It sounds like you're going through something incredibly painful right now, and I'm glad you said something. You don't have to go through this alone.

Please reach out right now: call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US), available 24/7.

If you're in immediate danger, please call 911.

New drooping on one side of the face or trouble closing one eye can be a sign of nerve involvement — which can occur in Lyme disease (facial/Bell's palsy) but also has other causes that need prompt evaluation.

Please be seen today: go to urgent care or an emergency room, or call your doctor's office now and describe these symptoms.
